doc.title: Scott Yanow interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 22, 2021

title: Opinion in reviews, skipping records, and loyalty to readers
summary: Opinion should be secondary to description; he skips non-jazz and answers to readers, not musicians or critics.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: So in those 30-word summarizing pattern, when you get into more lengthy reviews, at what point does your personal opinion start to enter into your writing?

Well there’s always a certain amount of that anyway because you have to edit it and you are — is it a favorable review or was the album a disappointment for one reason or another? You know there’s a certain amount of that, but that should be secondary to just describing what it sounds like and being accurate you know in order to describe it right, and for the readers, you know it’s up to them, to a certain extent, to maybe read a few other things from each writer to get an idea of whether their taste is similar to yours. Because a lot of times I’ll read stuff and I’ll know that maybe this is an album that I would like but the writer, the journalist, obviously doesn’t like it. You know they write it off, they’re not into swing, and I’ll say well, he’s saying it’s a swing record so maybe it’ll be interesting to me. You know so, you know there should be enough clues in the reviews so the reader will have an idea.
Have you ever had occasion to dislike a record so much that you pass on the review?

Once in a great while. If it’s not jazz, if it’s outside of jazz or say it’s a rap record or something, then I won’t even review it. And if it’s a situation, which is true of several of the magazines I write for where I get to choose what I’d like to review, if I put it on and it’s kind of dull then I think well maybe some other time and I’ll switch to another record. But if you’re assigned something, like say for DownBeat or Jazz-Is then I pretty much have to review it, but in most cases they assign me things that are complementary to my tastes anyway.

Okay. Some of our best known and iconic musicians, jazz musicians, have taken a turn at trying to enter the pop market or become more popular. Have you had instances where you’re reviewing some of our heroes and all of a sudden they’re covering Beatles songs or something like that?

Well they’ll do that once in a while, and I don’t blame them for trying to make some more money, but on the other hand you know my responsibility is really towards my readers. It’s not towards musicians, it’s certainly not toward other critics. Because sometimes you read something from a journalist and they’re obviously trying to impress, you know, other writers. Or they’re trying to cozy up to musicians. But no, I don’t, I want the readers to know that if they’re going to spend fifteen or twenty dollars on a CD it’ll most likely be something that they’ll like, or something that’s at least in a style of music that interests them.
